title: Honoring your parents
hook: Becoming Muslim didn't make you owe your parents less. It made you owe them more.

screens.text: Your parents may not share your faith. They may not even understand it. But Islam gives them a place in your life that nothing can take away, and it grows as they get older.
A man asked the Prophet ﷺ who most deserved his good company. His answer: your mother. And next? Your mother. And next? Your mother again. Only then, your father [Bukhari 5971].
bubbles: That list has no religion test.
Allah tells us to keep our parents company in this world with kindness, even when they don't share our faith [Q 31:14–15].
What you don't follow is a push to disobey Allah, like worshipping other than Him [Q 31:15].

screens.prompt: Kindness always, with one exception. Sort these.

items.text: Calling to check on your mom
items.why: Yes. Her faith doesn't change her right to your good company [Q 31:15].

items.text: Driving your dad to a doctor's appointment
items.why: Yes. Real help in daily life is honoring him.

items.text: Being pushed to worship other than Allah
items.why: That's the one thing you don't follow [Q 31:15]. And even then, you stay kind.

items.text: Listening to the same story told twice
items.why: Yes. Patience with small things is where honoring is lived.

items.text: Being told to give up praying
items.why: Obeying stops where it means disobeying Allah. Say no gently, and stay warm.{teen} Under 18? Talk to {{mentor.name}} first.{/teen}

screens.text: **As they get older.** The Qur'an speaks to this moment: when one or both parents reach old age in your care, don't even say "ugh" to them. Speak with honor, lower yourself to them out of mercy, and pray for them [Q 17:23–24].
bubbles: Notice where it starts: *old age, in your care.* The repeated questions, the slow walks, the stubbornness. That's exactly where this is meant to be lived.

screens.situation: Keisha's dad, 71 and not Muslim, needs more help after a stroke. Her siblings say: "You're the religious one now, so you take him." Keisha works full-time and has two kids.

options.text: Take on a real share she can keep up (appointments, weekly visits, meals) and ask her siblings to split the rest
options.feedback: Yes. Honoring him means steady, real care. A plan she can sustain will serve him better than one she burns out on.

options.text: Move him in and do everything herself, to prove Islam made her better
options.feedback: Generous, but burning out helps nobody. Allah doesn't ask more than you can bear [Q 2:286]. Share the load.

options.text: Tell her siblings it's on them, since he isn't Muslim
options.feedback: Not quite. His faith doesn't cancel his rights. Kindness to non-Muslim parents is a command [Q 31:15].

options.text: Send money each month but stay out of the rest
options.feedback: Money helps, and some seasons that's what you can give. But if you can, your presence matters to him too.

screens.title: Questions converts ask about their parents

cards.front: "Can I make du'a for my parents if they're not Muslim?"
cards.back: Yes. Pray for their guidance, health and happiness, by name. Abu Hurayrah asked the Prophet ﷺ to pray for his mother's guidance [Muslim 2491].

cards.front: "Do I have to obey them in everything?"
cards.back: Respect and kindness, always. Go along with what they ask when it's good and reasonable, never when it means disobeying Allah [Q 31:15]. Even then, say no gently.

cards.front: "They mock my faith. Do I still owe them kindness?"
cards.back: Yes. Asma' kept good ties with her mother, who wasn't Muslim, and the Prophet ﷺ told her to [Bukhari 2620].

cards.front: "What if a parent dies before accepting Islam?"
cards.back: That's a heavy question, and you're allowed to grieve fully. Day 77 covers it gently. Your imam is there too.

steps.text: Call more than you used to, and listen.
Show up for doctor visits, moves, birthdays and hospital stays.
Help with money when they need it, as much as you're able.
Be patient with the same story told twice.
Keep your salah steady, but never let it become an excuse to skip time with them.

screens.text: **Your safety comes first.** If home ever feels unsafe, Day 14's steps still apply. Honoring your parents never means putting yourself in danger.
bubbles: {teen}Under 18 and living at home? Honoring your parents looks like a respectful tone, doing your chores without being asked, and keeping house rules.{/teen}
{teen}The one exception is anything that means disobeying Allah, like being told never to pray. Don't fight that alone: talk to {{mentor.name}} first.{/teen}

screens.prompt: Which best describes what Islam asks toward non-Muslim parents?

options.text: Kindness and good company always; obey them except in disobeying Allah
options.feedback: Right. Their faith doesn't change their right to your kindness [Q 31:15].

options.text: Distance yourself until they accept Islam
options.feedback: Not quite. The Qur'an tells you to keep them company in this world with kindness [Q 31:15].

options.text: Obey them in everything, including religion
options.feedback: Not quite. Kindness always, but you don't follow a push away from worshipping Allah [Q 31:15].

chips: How do I care for a parent who's getting older and sicker?
My mom wants me to take her to church. What do I do?
My parent was abusive. Do I still have to keep in touch?
What's a good du'a for my parents?

screens.text: Call or visit a parent today (or the person who raised you), only if it's safe for you.
steps: Ask how they're really doing, and listen
Ask one thing you could help with this week
screens.optional_extra: Make du'a for each of your parents by name tonight: their health, their happiness and their guidance.

screens.text: Your parents have a right to your kindness whatever their faith, and that right grows as they age. Obey them in everything except disobeying Allah, and say even that gently.
Every phone call and every patient answer counts with Allah.

check.prompt: Who did the Prophet ﷺ name three times as most deserving of your good company?

options.feedback: Right. Your mother three times, then your father [Bukhari 5971].
Not quite. He said your mother, three times, then your father [Bukhari 5971].

check.prompt: Your non-Muslim parent asks you to do something that disobeys Allah. What does the Qur'an say?

options.text: Don't obey that, but keep treating them kindly
options.feedback: Right. Kindness stays even when you say no [Q 31:15].
Not quite. Decline that one thing, and keep them company with kindness [Q 31:15].

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- The mother three times, then the father, are most deserving of good company [Bukhari 5971].
- Good treatment of parents comes right after worshipping Allah alone; in their old age: no "uff," noble speech, humility out of mercy, du'a [Q 17:23–24].
- Non-Muslim parents keep their right to kindness; don't obey a push toward shirk, but keep their company in this world with kindness [Q 31:14–15]. Asma' was told to keep ties with her non-Muslim mother [Bukhari 2620].
- A new Muslim's family keeps binding rights: courtesy and respect are required; avoid religious arguments; obey parents except in disobedience to Allah [Revealed Path ch. 21].
- Caregiving should be sustainable; Allah doesn't burden a soul beyond its capacity [Q 2:286].
- Convert evidence: family is a top worry, and converts carry relationships with non-Muslim parents for decades [Research Notes - Retention and Convert Voices].

**Likely questions**
- *"How do I care for an aging parent?"* Practical help: a shared family plan, appointments, a routine of calls and visits, local senior services, respite for the carer. Kindness in small daily things counts.
- *"Can I pray for my non-Muslim parents?"* Yes: for their guidance, health and well-being, while they're alive. Questions about praying for a parent who has died go to Day 77 and the imam (Q23).
- *"My mom wants me to drive her to church / help her with her religious practice."* (scholar question Q30) Don't rule. Give the cautious picture: you keep helping her in every part of daily life, and you don't take part in the worship itself; whether helping with getting there (a ride, a wheelchair) is fine is a question scholars discuss, so offer "Ask my imam." Never suggest refusing in a way that harms the relationship.
- *"My parent was abusive."* Honoring parents never requires putting yourself in danger. Keeping a safe distance while staying civil can be part of it. Route to the imam and mentor; follow the safety rule if there's current danger.
- *"Good du'a for parents?"* The Qur'an's own: *"My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up [when I was] small"* [Q 17:24, Saheeh Intl.]. For non-Muslim parents who are alive, praying for their guidance is the clearest gift; Abu Hurayrah asked the Prophet ﷺ to pray for his mother's guidance [Muslim 2491].

**Escalate:** the church-ride question and any request to take part in a parent's religious practice; inheritance from or to a non-Muslim parent; end-of-life and funeral arrangements; abusive or unsafe parents; a teen whose parents forbid prayer or Islam (mentor and imam, safeguarding rules).

**Don't**
- Don't suggest a parent's faith reduces their rights.
- Don't predict anyone's afterlife.
- Don't coach a minor to defy or deceive their parents (Spec §6.2 rule 12).
